pages.name: Building a New Starship
pages.html:
Building a New Starship

Building a new starship: Spacers can commission a new starship by taking out a loan and selecting a pre-constructed ship or hiring a naval architect to design one.

  • Downpayment: 20% of the starship's new price is required for a downpayment to get a loan for a starship. If commissioning a stock model, the overall cost of construction decreases by 10% due to the routine setup to fabricate.
  • Naval architect: Hiring a naval architect allows the spacer to design the layout and components of their ship instead of purchasing a stock model. Hiring an architect costs 1% of the ship's final cost and takes one month of work to draft plans.
  • Shipyard: Shipyards are typically found in starports class A and B.
  • Construction time: Construction takes between 10-36 months to complete.

Book p.74

pages.name: Starship Design Procedure
pages.html:
Starship Design Procedure

  • 1) Determine Hull
  • 2) Determine Engineering: J-drive, M-drive, and Power Plant
  • 3) Determine Bridge: controls, computer, and weapons controls
  • 4) Determine Life Support System: Staterooms and low passage berths
  • 5) Determine Fuel Allotment and Space
  • 6) Determine Weaponry
  • 7) Optional: Secondary Spacecraft
  • 8) Determine Cargo Capacity
  • 9) Determine Cost and Time

Book p.74

pages.name: 1) Hulls
pages.html:
1) Hulls

Hulls: Hulls are the main body of the starship and are represented in displacement tonnes.

  • Hull size: This is one of the main six commonly found hull types available at starports. It is possible to request hull sizes outside of this range, but will be considered “custom” built and take 36 months to construct.
  • Main space: This represents the amount of available space to use when installing ship components such as state rooms and determining cargo space.
  • Engines: This is the required amount of displacement tonnes reserved for engineering systems such as the drive systems and power plant.
  • Cost: This column is the base cost of construction. Custom hull construction outside of the provided amount is 100Kcr per additional 1 tonne.
  • Construction Time: This is the typical construction time of a ship of this hull size. Custom ships always will take 36 months regardless of size.

pages.name: 2) Engineering
pages.html:
2) Engineering

Engineering: All ships need the following systems to be considered functional.

  • Jump Drive (J-Drive): Determines the amount of parsecs the Jump Drive can jump.
  • Maneuver Drive (M-Drive): Determines the speed of the ship when in normal space.
  • Power plant (POW): Determines the power output of the ship, which can limit the potential of the installed J-Drive and M-Drive if the Power Plant rating is lower than required by the drives.

All ships have a rating which correlates to its maximum output as determined by hull size. Only one of each engineering component may be installed on a ship, up to the maximum amount of space available by hull size.

  • Damage: When any drive or the power plant is damaged due to attack or poor maintenance, it decreases one rating, which will in turn limit the ability of the ship to jump, maneuver, or supply power.
  • Example: If a 100T ship’s B-class M-Drive is hit, it decreases from B to A, limiting the amount of Gs it can produce from 4 to 2. If the M-drive is damaged further, it is considered destroyed and cannot function anymore, making the ship incapable of producing any more thrust.

pages.name: 3) The Bridge
pages.html:
3) The Bridge

The Bridge: The bridge will always use 20T of space for all of the essential functions of the ship. A computer system must be installed on the bridge, for the operation of the ship. The bridge costs 500Kcr per 100T hull.

  • Computer: The ship’s computer will provide the main functions of the ship along with an amount of bandwidth slots capable of additional computer functions the spacer can program and customize as desired, with computer modules.
  • #bis: This indicates that the computer has a built-in Astrogator program for automatically processing jump points. The number indicates the amount of jump routes it can process at once for the installed j-drive.

Book p.75

pages.name: 4) Life Support
pages.html:
4) Life Support

  • Staterooms: Staterooms are necessary to provide living space for the crew and passengers. Staterooms are fitted with the necessary life support systems such as air recycling, plumbing, heat, etc., as well as personal storage and installed furnishings. Each 4 tonnes of space costs 500Kcr.
  • Low berth: Low berth provides space for transporting people in suspended animation and as such have minimal space requirements. A single berth costs 50Kcr and displaces 0.5 tonnes.

Book p.75

pages.name: 5) Fuel
pages.html:
5) Fuel

Fuel: A ship’s fuel requires a minimum amount of allotted space, equal to 10% of the hull.

  • J-Drive usage: The J-Drive requires an amount of fuel equal to the POW rating by hull type x 10. For example, a 200T starship with a B-class J-Drive (rating of 2) requires 20T of fuel to jump its maximum distance.
  • M-Drive usage: A ship’s M-Drive requires an amount of fuel equal to the POW max by hull type to operate for a week. For example, a 200T ship with a B-class M-drive requires 2T of fuel per week to operate.
  • Operational systems: A ship requires 1 tonne of fuel per 100T to operate for a month. For example, a 200T ship requires 2T of fuel per month to maintain the ship’s systems. Most ships provide enough room for fuel that equals the required amount for a maximum jump plus the amount needed for one month of M-Drive and one month of life support.
  • Example: A 200T starship with a B-class J-Drive will have 20T of fuel space for the jumps. To operate the B-class M-drive, it will have an additional 8T of fuel space, along with 2T for operational systems, totalling 30T of fuel space needed.
  • Fuel Space Mapping: When drawing deck plans, fuel will usually be stored within the fuselage areas not being used by staterooms or cargo as long as there is adequate space. Otherwise external fuel containers may need to be attached.

Book p.76

pages.name: 6) Weapons
pages.html:
6) Weapons

Weapons: Weapons require hardpoints in order to be installed. Each ship's hull comes with 1 hardpoint per 100T of hull. Additional hardpoints can be installed, up to x2 the hull’s original hardpoint, at 50,000cr each.

  • Turret: A turret costs 100Kcr and deals 1 damage. Turrets are able to fire in a 180 degree area, with a gunner. Otherwise, with no gunner, they are considered fixed mounted.
  • Pulse: Costs 500kcr and inflicts D3 damage.
  • Beam: Costs 1Mcr and deals 1 damage, but deals +1 for every additional round the beam maintains contact on the target ship. For example, if the beam maintains contact on the third round, it deals 3 damage that round. Beams have a chance to overheat. Each round, roll 1D. A roll of 1 on the first round causes it to overheat, while on the second round of use, a 2 or less causes it to overheat, and so on. The Gunner Skill is added to this overheat roll to offset the chances. When a beam overheats, it requires a number of rounds of cooling equal to the number of rounds it was in use.
  • Missile Rack: The missile rack costs 750kcr and can hold up to 4 missiles. A missile rack can fire between 1-4 missiles in a single attack. Each missile costs 1,000cr and deals 1 damage. Missiles impact a number of rounds later equal to the amount of range bands between attacker and defender.
  • Sandcasters: This countermeasure provides a -4DM to beam weapon attacks and -2DM to missiles. Each canister dispenser costs 250Kcr and can fit 4 canisters.

Book p.76

pages.name: 7) Secondary Spacecraft
pages.html:
7) Optional: Secondary Spacecraft

Optional: Secondary Spacecraft: All secondary craft have 1 hull point.

  • Escape boat: This is a small ship used to escape a ship in case of emergency. It takes up 20T of space, and 3 passengers and 20 emergency low berth pods can be crammed inside. An escape boat has 5T of fuel and isn’t armed. Each pod costs 14Mcr.
  • Ship’s boat: This is a 5-passenger small craft that is 30T, has up to 12T of cargo space, has 9T of fuel, and is capable of 6G of thrust. This ship is used for short trips, boarding, and mining. The ship doesn't have hardpoints but can have one pulse or beam installed as a fixed mounted weapon that takes 2T of space. A ship’s boat costs 16Mcr.
  • Pinnace: This craft is a 40T version of a ship’s boat, with 12T of fuel and 12T of cargo. It can hold up to 8 passengers. This ship also has one pulse beam fixed mounted onto the fore of the craft. A pinnace costs 20Mcr.
  • Cutter: This ship is a larger version of a pinnace, at 50T, and carries up to 12 passengers while travelling at 4Gs. Cutters are capable of planetary landings and may be constructed to be modular, so they can have different modules installed for specific tasks. A cutter comes equipped with one beam laser and has 15 tonnes of cargo space. A cutter costs 28Mcr.
  • Shuttle: A shuttle is designed for planetary landings but also as an intra-system spacecraft. The shuttle can carry 30 passengers, has 3Gs of thrust, weighs 95 tons, and can carry 80T of cargo. Shuttles are not equipped with weapons and cost 33Mcr.
  • Fighter: A fighter is a small, 10T craft with 6Gs of acceleration, designed for close-ranged ship combat. Each fighter can only carry one passenger, has two pulse lasers mounted, and has either three missile racks or three sandcasters. A fighter is only capable of short operation times between 1 hour at 6Gs (skirmish) and up to 6 hours at one 1G (patrol), and carries up to 1T of cargo and 1T of fuel. The cost of a fighter is 18Mcr.

All non-starship spacecraft consume 1/100T (10kg) of fuel per ten minutes of operation at 1G. This rate of consumption increases equal to the number of Gs they are operating at. Small spacecraft are not capable of jumping.

  • For example, a ship’s boat travelling at 6Gs consumes 6/100T (60kg) per ten minutes. This will allow it to operate for 1500 minutes (25 hours) due to it having 9T of fuel.

Small Craft Damage: All small craft have hull 1 and cockpit 1. Weapons provide 1 hit per installed weapon, and the drive provides a number of hits equal to thrust.

  • Hull damage: When the hull is at 0 hits, any additional hits destroy the ship.
  • Cockpit damage: When the cockpit is hit, the pilot takes 2D damage. Additional hits destroy the cockpit, with any additional damage hitting the hull.
  • Weapon damage: Any hit to weapons disables a weapon system. If all weapons are disabled, then all other weapon damage hits the hull.
  • Drive damage: When the drive hits 0 hits, the craft cannot maneuver anymore. Any additional hits explode the drive system and fuel, destroying the ship.

Book p.76-77

pages.name: 8) Determining Cargo Capacity
pages.html:
8) Determine Cargo Capacity

Determine Cargo Capacity: Once all of the mandatory space has been allotted on the ship, determine the remaining cargo space that the spacers can use to transport goods or their own supplies. The following can be placed into storage:

  • Repair parts: Spare parts cost 100,000cr per tonne. Repair parts are used to fix malfunctions or damaged ship systems, including the hull. Repair parts come with 10 uses, where each repair will use 1/10th of the repair parts (1/10 tonnes) per 1 damage. Critical repairs require using the full tonne of spare parts to get the system out of critical condition. Malfunctions use 1D of the repair parts to fix.
  • Missiles: Individual missiles cost 5000Cr and are homing.
  • Sandcaster Canisters: Each sand canister refill costs 500Cr.
  • Vehicles: Planet-side vehicles are stored in the cargo bay, typically, but some starships may have specialized ports for them.

Book p.77

pages.name: Ship Modifications
pages.html:
Ship Modifications

Hull Streamlining: Streamlining a starship allows it to fly in an atmosphere without penalty.

  • Streamlining a starship costs 1Mcr per 100T.
  • Operating a non-streamlined starship in an atmosphere incurs -2DM.

Fuel Scoops: Required for harvesting hydrogen off of gas giants. 1Mcr.

Refinery Module: Unprocessed fuel can be refined to remove any contaminants, to make it less likely to cause problems. 2.5Mcr and weighs 5T.

  • Refining time: 5T per hour.
  • Increase refinement amount: Multiple refineries can be installed to double or triple the amount of fuel that can be processed.

Armour: Armour can be installed on a ship to help defend different parts of a starship from taking damage. Armour reduces the damage to the hit area of a starship by -1.

  • Cost: Armour costs 100Kcr per -1DMG.
  • Armor can be installed on the following areas: Hull, M-Drive, J-Drive, Power, Fuel, and Internal.
  • Armor placement: A ship can have multiple layers of armor installed in the same area to further reduce taken damage in an area by additional -1.
  • Armor limit: A Ship can only have 1 armor installed per 100T. If more is installed, it will impact the ship’s performance, with the ship considered the next displacement tonnage category. For example, having two armor installed on a 100T ship will effectively make it perform as a 200T ship—impacting its M-Drive, J-Drive, and power plant.
  • Destroyed armour: If the attacking ship rolls a 12+, then the armour absorbs the damage but is destroyed in the process. Destroyed armour cannot be repaired.

Weapon Variants:

  • Double turret: A turret with two barrels is 400Kcr and deals 2 damage.
  • Triple turret: A turret with three barrels is 800kcr and deals 3 damage.
  • EMP missiles: This type of missile is used to temporarily disable the power system of a ship. Each missile puts the target’s power plant offline for 1D 10-minute rounds and costs 5,000cr.

Book p.77

pages.name: Ship Computer
pages.html:
Ship Computer

A ship will have a computer, needed for basic starship operations. All computers have a number of available installation slots and bandwidth for running each installed program module.

  • Module slots: Each slot can be filled by a program module, in the form of a cartridge or memory stick. It is possible to have more program modules than there are available on the computer, where the spacers must indicate which are currently installed in the ship's computer and which are not.
  • Bandwidth: Each program on a program module will require a certain amount of bandwidth to run.

A computer will often have multiple program modules installed but will only run certain ones as needed due to bandwidth limitations. It is possible to have additional program modules available that can be swapped in.

Computer programs are modules that are installed into the computer to provide assistance to starship operation.

Program Descriptions:

  • Library: Provides all common information on any subject in the subsector. Using the library to find information takes 1D hours to learn one fact. Common topics are the planetary data, government officials, settlements, animals, cultural customs, etc. Library data will also include popular jump routes and their jump points within the subsector, such as major trade routes. Library data can be updated with more information anytime a spacer travels to a new subsector, with the data costing 100kcr. It is easily available in any starports A-C.

Writing Computer Programs: A spacer can choose to write their own program. Typically, these programs can be used to mimic a Skill that a programmer themself has. However, programs are entirely up to the programmer to develop and can be totally unique applications of a computer, as the referee allows. Assume all programs take 1 bandwidth of processing, but the referee can add more if the use of the program needs to be balanced with regards to its capabilities. Any program written to mimic a Skill rank requires 1 bandwidth per two Skill ranks.

  • Writing time: Each program requires four dedicated weeks per single function it is being written to perform. If the program is duplicating a Skill level, it requires eight weeks per additional Skill level to program.
  • Program testing: Once a computer program is done being written, then it is tested. The programmer must succeed on an INT-modified Computer check, with a 8+ result to succeed. If the program is written to mimic a Skill higher than the programmer’s expertise, then apply a -1DM to the roll per rank above the programmer’s knowledge. If a failure occurs, an additional week of programming is needed per every -1 effect of the result before the program is usable.
  • Fatal flaw: If a failed result occurs, the referee rolls a hidden 2D roll and applies the negative effect amount. If the result is 2 or less, the program has a major bug in it regardless of additional programming time but that only becomes apparent at a stressful situation where the program is used. This kink can be debugged once it has been discovered.
